record.label: Nonnegative certificate variables and zero expected divergence
record.statement: At a fixed positive time in a positive step with the preceding smooth profiles, define R=r^2, K=rs, b=-w/r, B=b-2v=-2H, j=s_x-(s/r)v, L=-r*s_xx, S=z+bv-2Rb=2rH_x. These extend evenly and smoothly, and R,K,v,B,j,L,S>=0. For D=r*partial_x and W(F)=D F+(v+R-K)F, the derivative rules in signs.tex give f W(F)=partial_x(r f F). For every polynomial F in R,K,v,b,j the terms are integrable, r f F vanishes at both infinities, and E_f W(F)=0.
record.boundary: Curated source-level mathematical statement, not an elaborated Lean extraction or independently accepted proof. Its displayed local hypotheses are quantified guards; a hypothetical plateau is not an added premise of the full-support theorem. The zero-flux conclusion is analytic. It is not implied by a symbolic polynomial identity; both signs and vanishing boundary flux are required. These auxiliary profiles are not asserted to converge for general gamma.

aligned_passages.text: The gap argument needs a property of the derivative $q'$, rather than convexity of the spatial function $\Phi$. We establish the following analytic input before using minimality. Let $\gamma\in\mathcal U$ be constant with value $c$ on an open interval $I\subset(0,1)$, and let $X$ be its diffusion started at zero. Then $$ \begin{cases} q'''(t)\ge \dfrac1{1000c^2} \mathbb E\bigl[(c\Phi_{xx}(t,X_t))^4\bigr]>0,&c>0,\\[4pt] q''(t)=\mathbb E[\Phi_{xxx}(t,X_t)^2]>0,&c=0, \end{cases}\qquad t\in I. $$ Thus $q'$ is strictly convex for $c>0$ and strictly increasing for $c=0$. The coefficient may jump outside $I$ and may be unbounded near one, provided it is nonnegative, nondecreasing, right-continuous and integrable. No support property or minimising assumption enters this statement. The positive-time restriction matters when a diffusion density is used; interval endpoints are handled later by continuity. [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1][fs-curv]. The proof has two stages. In §§4.1–4.4 the coefficient is a positive monotone finite-step function with smooth terminal data. Shape comparisons and boundary estimates justify the [polynomial correction](#curvature-algebra) and its zero expectation. In [§4.5](#plateau-limit), approximants $\gamma_n,\Phi_n,X^n$ approach an arbitrary admissible coefficient. Only the integrated expression in spatial derivatives passes to the limit; the auxiliary forward scores need not converge. Bounds depend on a fixed compact strip and a common coefficient mass bound. The strictly positive right side is then justified for the limiting solution itself. ### 4.1 Why the uncorrected expression has no pointwise sign On a positive constant interval put $r=c\Phi_x$, $v=r_x$, $w=r_{xx}$ and $z=r_{xxx}$. In forward time, $r_t=-\tfrac12r_{xx}-rr_x$ and $dX_t=r(t,X_t)\,dt+dB_t$. Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's formula gives $$ dr(t,X_t)=v(t,X_t)\,dB_t, $$ $$ dv(t,X_t)=-v(t,X_t)^2\,dt+w(t,X_t)\,dB_t, \qquad dw(t,X_t)=-3v(t,X_t)w(t,X_t)\,dt+z(t,X_t)\,dB_t. $$ Since $q'=c^{-2}\mathbb E v^2$, the drift of $v^2$ yields $c^2q''=\mathbb E(w^2-2v^3)$. The drifts of $w^2$ and $v^3$ are, respectively, $z^2-6vw^2$ and $3vw^2-3v^4$. Therefore $$ c^2q'''=\mathbb E\bigl[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4\bigr]. $$ These are interior-time identities. On a smaller constant interval the heat formula gives classical time smoothness and bounded spatial derivatives of sufficiently high order, so the local martingale terms have zero mean and the expectation differentiations are justified. Nothing here assigns a sign to $q''$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.3][fs-reg]. There is a concrete obstruction to reading the last display pointwise. For the smooth finite-step problem $c=M=1$ on $[0,1)$, with terminal value $\log(2\cosh x)$, the exact solution is $$ \Phi(t,x)=\log(2\cosh x)+\frac{1-t}{2},\qquad r=\tanh x. $$ Indeed, $\Phi_{xx}+\Phi_x^2=1$. Writing $R=r^2$ gives $v=1-R$, $w=-2rv$ and $z=-2v^2+4Rv$. At $R=1/2$, $v=1/2$, $w^2=1/2$ and $z=1/2$, so $$ z^2-12vw^2+6v^4=-\frac{19}{8}<0. $$ This example lies in the smooth analytic class used below. Its diffusion density is $f_t(x)=e^{-t/2}\cosh(x)p_t(x)$, obtained from the heat transition formula, and integrates to one because $\mathbb E\cosh(B_t)=e^{t/2}$. It illustrates the necessity of the integration argument; it uses a smooth terminal value and makes no claim to be the zero-temperature minimiser. The displayed negative value is an exact elementary calculation. The heat formula itself is [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 2.1][fs-reg]. The same pointwise obstruction occurs with the actual terminal datum $|x|$. For the admissible constant coefficient $\gamma_c\equiv c>0$, write $\tau=1-t>0$ and use the same heat formula: $$ \Phi_c(t,x)=c^{-1}\log\mathbb E e^{c|x+\sqrt\tau Z|}. $$ At $c=0$ its continuous extension is the heat value, whose derivatives are $$ a_0=\sqrt{\frac2{\pi\tau}}e^{-x^2/(2\tau)},\qquad b_0=-\frac{x}{\tau}a_0,\qquad d_0=\left(\frac{x^2}{\tau^2}-\frac1\tau\right)a_0. $$ At $x=\sqrt\tau$, $d_0=0$ and $b_0^2=a_0^2/\tau>0$. For fixed $t,x$, Gaussian convolution may be differentiated in $x$ through its kernel and expanded in $c$ near zero: exponential moments dominate every resulting polynomial factor. The apparent singularity of $c^{-1}\log\mathbb E e^{c|x+\sqrt\tau Z|}$ is removable, and its spatial derivatives through order four are smooth in $c$. Hence $$ d_c^2-12c a_cb_c^2+6c^2a_c^4 =-\frac{12a_0^3}{\tau}c+O(c^2)<0 $$ for all sufficiently small positive $c$, at that fixed point. This is an ordinary consequence of the constant-coefficient formula, not an arbitrary assignment of unrelated derivative values. It neither asserts minimality of $\gamma_c$ nor contradicts the positive expectation proved below; it shows why that expectation cannot be replaced by a pointwise inequality even in the absolute-value-terminal model. ### 4.2 The smooth finite-step problem and its boundary control Take $0=t_0<\cdots ### 4.3 Backward and forward comparisons, including jumps Use backward time $\tau$ on a single step. The equation is $r_\tau=\tfrac12r_{xx}+rr_x$. The logarithmic heat formula preserves strict positivity of $v$: its second spatial derivative is the tilted mean of the old second derivative plus the tilted variance of the old first derivative. Initially $v=cM\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)>0$, and positive rescaling at a backward jump preserves this property. Consequently $r(x)>0$ for $x>0$. Twice differentiating gives $w_\tau=\tfrac12w_{xx}+rw_x+3vw$. At the terminal endpoint $w=-2cM^2\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)\tanh(Mx)\le0$ for $x>0$. The boundary value at zero is zero, and the differentiated tails make the far boundary tend uniformly to zero. Comparison applied to $-w$ gives $w\le0$ on the positive half-line. Define $$ H=\frac{r_\tau}{r}=\frac{w}{2r}+v. $$ Oddness and $r_x(0)=v(0)>0$ make $w/r$, hence $H$, smooth and even at zero. Direct differentiation gives $$ H_\tau=\tfrac12H_{xx}+(v/r+r)H_x+vH, $$ $$ (H_x)_\tau=\tfrac12(H_x)_{xx}+(v/r+r)(H_x)_x +((v/r)_x+2v)H_x+wH. $$ The terminal signs are $H=(cM-M^2)\operatorname{sech}^2(Mx)\le0$ and $H_x\ge0$ on $x>0$, using $M\ge c$. For the first comparison write $v/r+r=1/x+\eta(x)$, where $\eta$ is smooth and odd near zero. The radial extension $H(|y|)$ to $\mathbb R^3$ turns $\tfrac12H_{xx}+x^{-1}H_x$ into $\tfrac12\Delta H$. It is smooth at the origin, as is the extra drift, and $H$ tends uniformly to zero at infinity. Comparison on expanding balls proves $H\le0$. For the second comparison, $wH\ge0$ and $(v/r)_x=w/r-v^2/r^2<0$, so the zeroth-order coefficient has upper bound $2\sup v$. On $[\varepsilon,A]$, the two lateral errors are $H_x(\varepsilon)=O(\varepsilon)$ and $H_x(A)=o_A(1)$, uniformly on the closed step. Taking $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ and $A\to\infty$ gives $H_x\ge0$. At a backward jump $r_{\rm new}=\alpha r_{\rm old}$ with $0<\alpha\le1$, $$ H_{\rm new}=H_{\rm old}-(1-\alpha)v_{\rm old},\qquad (H_x)_{\rm new}=(H_x)_{\rm old}-(1-\alpha)w_{\rm old}. $$ Thus both signs survive every jump. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.2][fs-signs]. For the forward score use $a_s=s_x$, temporarily distinguishing it from the Hessian $a=\Phi_{xx}$. The forward heat equation gives $$ s_t=\tfrac12s_{xx}-ss_x,\qquad (a_s)_t=\tfrac12(a_s)_{xx}-s(a_s)_x-a_s^2, $$ $$ (s_{xx})_t=\tfrac12(s_{xx})_{xx}-s(s_{xx})_x-3a_s s_{xx}. $$ The first step has $s=x/t$. Thereafter $a_s-1/t$ satisfies the linear equation with drift $-s$ and zeroth-order coefficient $-(a_s+1/t)$. For fixed smooth data this coefficient is bounded above on a closed step, independently of spatial truncation; this uses the tail bound and continuity, before asserting its sign. Comparison gives $a_s\ge1/t$. The last displayed equation then gives $s_{xx}\le0$ on $x>0$. At a forward jump, $$ s_+=s_-+\delta\Phi_x,\quad (a_s)_+=(a_s)_-+\delta\Phi_{xx},\quad (s_{xx})_+=(s_{xx})_-+\delta\Phi_{xxx}. $$ The backward signs and $\delta\ge0$ preserve the forward signs. A further comparison, not concavity alone, is needed. On $x>0$ set $d_s=s_x/s$, $d_r=r_x/r$ and $\rho=d_s-d_r$. The heat equation gives $s_t=\tfrac12s_{xx}-ss_x$, whereas $r_t=-rH$. Taking logarithmic derivatives yields $$ (d_s)_t=\tfrac12(d_s)_{xx}+d_s(d_s)_x-s_{xx},\qquad (d_r)_t=-H_x. $$ Since $\tfrac12(d_r)_{xx}+d_r(d_r)_x=\tfrac12(w/r)_x=H_x-w$, substitution of $d_s=d_r+\rho$ gives its equation $$ \rho_t=\tfrac12\rho_{xx}+d_s\rho_x+(d_r)_x\rho +2H_x-w-s_{xx}. $$ All three terms in the source are nonnegative by the comparisons already proved, and $(d_r)_x<0$. On the first step, concavity gives $r(x)=\int_0^xv(y)\,dy\ge xv(x)$, so $\rho=1/x-v/r\ge0$. Odd Taylor expansions give $d_s=1/x+O(x)$, $d_r=1/x+O(x)$ and $\rho=O(x)$ near zero; the tail estimates give $\rho\to0$ at infinity. Comparison on $[\varepsilon,A]$ therefore proves $\rho\ge0$ on each subsequent step provided its initial sign is preserved. Define $$ j=s\rho=s_x-(s/r)v. $$ At a forward jump, with $\alpha=c_+/c_-$ and $\lambda=(c_+-c_-)/c_-$, $r_+=\alpha r_-$, $v_+=\alpha v_-$, $s_+=s_-+\lambda r_-$ and $(s_x)_+=(s_x)_-+\lambda v_-$. Substitution cancels the added terms and gives $j_+=j_-$. Since $s_+>0$ on $x>0$, the sign of $\rho$ is preserved. The quotient $s/r$ extends smoothly and evenly across zero, with $j(0)=0$; reflection gives $j\ge0$ everywhere. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.3][fs-signs]. ### 4.4 How the signs make a correction with zero expectation useful Here the coefficient is a positive constant $c$ on the step containing the chosen time. The variables are the rescaled spatial derivatives $$ r=c\Phi_x,\qquad v=c\Phi_{xx},\qquad w=c\Phi_{xxx},\qquad z=c\Phi_{xxxx}. $$ Write $h=e^{c\Phi}$ and factor the forward diffusion density as $f=hg$; its auxiliary score is $s=-\partial_x\log g$. These are the backward and forward quantities compared in §4.3. On the positive half-line, where $r,s>0$, set $$ H=\frac{w}{2r}+v,\qquad j=s_x-\frac{s}{r}v,\qquad \rho=\frac{s_x}{s}-\frac vr, \qquad j=s\rho. $$ In this certificate only, $b=-w/r$ is a quotient; it is not the derivative $\Phi_{xxx}$ denoted by $b$ in the unscaled curvature formula. At a fixed positive time inside the step define $$ R=r^2,\quad K=rs,\quad b=-w/r,\quad B=b-2v, \quad L=-rs_{xx},\quad S_1=z+bv-2Rb. $$ The subscript on $S_1$ distinguishes it from the support set. The previous comparisons give $$ R,K,v,B,j,L,S_1\ge0,\qquad b=B+2v\ge0,\qquad Rb^2=w^2, $$ because $B=-2H$ and $S_1=2rH_x$. Here $s=-\partial_x\log g$ belongs to the forward heat factor, while $\partial_x\log f=r-s$ is the logarithmic derivative of the diffusion density. The signs have separate sources: $B\ge0$ comes from $H\le0$, $S_1\ge0$ from $H_x\ge0$ on the positive half-line, $j=s\rho\ge0$ from the relative-slope comparison, and $L=-rs_{xx}\ge0$ from forward concavity. Reflection extends these signs. The quotients were defined for $x>0$, where $r>0$ and $v>0$ by the tilted mean-and-variance argument in [§4.3](#shape-comparisons). At zero, $r$ and $w$ are odd, $r_x(0)=v(0)>0$, and division by $r$ is therefore division by a function with a simple zero. This gives the smooth even extension $b(0)=-z(0)/v(0)$; the other comparison identities give $j(0)=0$ and $S_1(0)=0$. Thus zero is not an omitted boundary of the integration. For $\mathcal D=r\partial_x$, direct differentiation gives $$ \mathcal D(R,K,v,b,j) =(2Rv,\ 2vK+Rj,\ -Rb,\ -z-bv,\ -jv+Kb-L). $$ Also $f_x/f=r-s$. Hence $\mathcal W(F)=\mathcal DF+(v+R-K)F$ satisfies $$ f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF). $$ This identity does not itself make the integral vanish. The tails give $r=O(1)$; exponential decay of $v,w,z,b$ and their derivatives; $s=x/t+O(1)$; $j=1/t+O((1+x)e^{-\kappa x})$; and $K=O(1+x)$. Every polynomial $F$ in $R,K,v,b,j$ and its differentiated expression therefore has at most polynomial growth. Meanwhile $f(t,x)\le C\exp(-x^2/(2t)+C|x|)$. Thus every term used below is absolutely integrable and $rfF\to0$ at both infinities. Smooth extension across zero prevents an interior boundary term. Integrating on $[-A,A]$ and taking $A\to\infty$ now gives $\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 3.4][fs-signs]. The proof has four separate checks: the comparisons supply these signs; the tail estimates make the correction integrate to zero; the rational identity below gives a positive remainder; and [§4.5](#plateau-limit) passes the resulting expectation inequality to the original coefficient. The polynomial check verifies the third step. Set $$ (A,C,k,T_0,g_0,h_0)= \left(\frac1{13},\frac{53}{24},\frac{19}{16},\frac{73}{48}, \frac{2331}{10000},\frac{87}{2500}\right), $$ $$ (x_0,y,m,n_0)= \left(\frac{4663}{5000},\frac{6853}{10000}, -\frac{1051}{400},-\frac{1073}{500}\right). $$ Define $$ Q=Avb+Cv^2+kKv-2kRb+T_0Rv,\qquad T_1=v(g_0R+h_0j), $$ $$ \begin{aligned} F_2={}&(Av-2kR)b^2 +b\bigl(2Cv^2+2kKv+(g_0+2T_0)Rv+h_0jv\bigr)\\ &+x_0v^2j+yv^3+mKv^2+n_0Rv^2. \end{aligned} $$ The choice is motivated by the terms containing $z$. In fact, $$ \begin{aligned} \partial_bF_2 &=2(Av-2kR)b+2Cv^2+2kKv+(g_0+2T_0)Rv+h_0jv\\ &=2Q+T_1,\\ {}[z]\mathcal W(F_2)&=-\partial_bF_2=-(2Q+T_1). \end{aligned} $$ Here $[z]$ means the coefficient of $z$; only $\mathcal Db=-z-bv$ contributes it. The square $(z+Q)^2$ and $S_1T_1$ contribute $2Q+T_1$, so these terms cancel exactly. Therefore subtracting $(z+Q)^2+S_1T_1+\mathcal W(F_2)$ from the curvature expression cancels every term involving $z$. The other favourable derivative is $\partial_jF_2=x_0v^2+h_0bv\ge0$: the $-L$ in $\mathcal Dj$ leaves a nonnegative correction. Put $$ \begin{aligned} P_0&=Rj(b-7v)^2,& P_1&=RB(b-\tfrac73v)^2,\\ P_2&=Kv(b-\tfrac92v)^2,& P_3&=vB(K+\tfrac14R-\tfrac17v)^2,\\ P_4&=(vb-\tfrac{14}{5}v^2-\tfrac{13}{4}Kv+\tfrac43Rv)^2, \end{aligned} $$ $$ (p_0,p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4)= \left(\frac{337}{10000},\frac{183}{2500},\frac{411}{10000}, \frac{11461}{5000},\frac{647}{10000}\right). $$ Exact expansion, with $b=B+2v$, gives $$ z^2-12Rvb^2+6v^4 =(z+Q)^2+S_1T_1+\sum_{i=0}^4p_iP_i +\mathcal W(F_2)+L(x_0v^2+h_0bv)+P_{\rm rem}. $$ For completeness, the entire remainder is specified by this table; every unlisted coefficient is zero. | Monomial | Coefficient | Monomial | Coefficient | | --- | ---: | --- | ---: | | $R^2v^2$ | $223/160000$ | $R^2vB$ | $4007/240000$ | | $R^2B^2$ | $1097/120000$ | $RKv^2$ | $83/80000$ | | $RKvB$ | $3343/24000$ | $Rv^3$ | $16259/23400000$ | | $Rv^2B$ | $30179/5460000$ | $Rv^2j$ | $26/625$ | | $RvB^2$ | $107/15000$ | $RvBj$ | $3/2500$ | | $RB^3$ | $121/32500$ | $RB^2j$ | $11/10000$ | | $K^2v^2$ | $579/20000$ | $K^2vB$ | $207/2500$ | | $Kv^3$ | $911/975000$ | $Kv^2B$ | $349/420000$ | | $Kv^2j$ | $5011/5000$ | $KvB^2$ | $133/130000$ | | $KvBj$ | $87/2500$ | $v^4$ | $1661507/1521000000$ | | $v^3B$ | $633799/621075000$ | $v^2B^2$ | $10657/1690000$ | All square prefactors $Rj,RB,Kv,vB,1$ are nonnegative, as are $S_1T_1$, $L(x_0v^2+h_0bv)$ and every remainder monomial. Integration removes only $\mathcal W(F_2)$, giving $$ \mathbb E_f[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4] \ge\frac{1661507}{1521000000}\mathbb E_fv^4 \ge\frac1{1000}\mathbb E_fv^4. $$ The surplus of the first coefficient over $1/1000$ is exactly $140507/1521000000>0$. The rational identity and positive table can be checked by finite arithmetic. Their application to this diffusion also uses the signs, quotient behaviour, integrability and vanishing flux proved above. Dividing the integrated inequality by $c^2$ returns $$ \mathbb E[\Phi_{xxxx}^2-12c\Phi_{xx}\Phi_{xxx}^2 +6c^2\Phi_{xx}^4] \ge\frac{c^2}{1000}\mathbb E\Phi_{xx}^4. $$ This is the unscaled estimate needed by the gap argument. Section 4.5 passes it to the original coefficient and supplies strictness for the limiting solution. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 4.1 and Proposition 4.2][fs-cert].

The quantity used in both arguments is a spatial moment. Recall $a=\Phi_{xx}$, write $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$, and, for $00$. For its associated diffusion, $$ \mathcal C_\gamma(t)\geq\frac{c^2}{1000} \mathbb E[a(t,X_t)^4]. $$ Neither minimality nor a constant neighbourhood of $t$ is required. This is the consequence of [OpenAI (2026a), Proposition 5.1 and Lemmas 2.1–2.2][FS] stated in the companion's [Proposition 4.1, §4.5](../long/reasoning-record.md#fixed-time-coercivity). We first explain the positive-plateau estimate, then obtain this fixed-time form by inserting a short plateau. For a smooth coefficient the identity connecting the two applications is $$ q'''+2\gamma'\mathbb E a^3=\mathcal C_\gamma. $$ On a plateau, $\gamma'=0$; at a smooth minimiser, full support gives $q=t$ and hence $q'''=0$. Section 4 proves the required smoothness before using the second identity. On a plateau with $\gamma=c>0$, put $r=c\Phi_x=c u$, $v=r_x=c a$, $w=r_{xx}$ and $z=r_{xxx}$. This rescaling makes the derivative identities polynomial. The PDE becomes $r_t=-\tfrac12r_{xx}-rr_x$, and the diffusion has spatial generator $\tfrac12\partial_{xx}+r\partial_x$. Differentiating in space and applying Itô's formula gives the drift and diffusion pairs $(0,v)$, $(-v^2,w)$ and $(-3vw,z)$ for $r,v,w$, respectively. All expectations in this section evaluate spatial functions at $(t,X_t)$. Starting with $c^2q'=\mathbb E v^2$, Itô's formula gives $$ \begin{aligned} c^2q''&=\mathbb E[w^2-2v^3],\\ c^2q'''&=\mathbb E[z^2-12vw^2+6v^4] =c^2\mathcal C_\gamma(t). \end{aligned} \tag{4} $$ For example, the drifts of $w^2$ and $v^3$ are $z^2-6vw^2$ and $3vw^2-3v^4$, respectively. The negative mixed term is the obstacle. Convexity, which gives $v\geq0$, does not control it. Indeed, for the smooth auxiliary terminal value $\log(2\cosh x)$ and coefficient $\gamma\equiv1$, the solution is $\Phi(t,x)=\log(2\cosh x)+(1-t)/2$. Thus $r=\tanh x$; at $r^2=1/2$, the polynomial in (4) equals $-19/8$. This is a finite-step smoothing example, not a minimiser of the absolute-value-terminal problem; its calculation is given in [long §4.1](../long/reasoning-record.md#curvature-moments). The same section gives a negative pointwise value with the actual $|x|$ terminal datum for a small positive constant coefficient ([long §4.1, pointwise obstruction](../long/reasoning-record.md#pointwise-curvature-obstruction)). The proof subtracts a weighted divergence whose expectation under the law of $X_t$ is zero. The resulting expression has a positive fourth-moment remainder. The backward value function and the forward density must satisfy joint shape restrictions for this decomposition to have the required signs. Those comparisons and the exact polynomial identity are the substantial inputs from [OpenAI (2026a), §§3–4][FS]. We explain their roles first for finite-step coefficients, then pass the integrated inequality to an integrable coefficient by approximation. Begin with a positive nondecreasing finite-step coefficient $\gamma_{\rm step}$: a function constant on each interval of a finite partition. Replace the terminal value $|x|$ by the smooth approximation $M^{-1}\log(2\cosh Mx)$, with $M\geq\|\gamma_{\rm step}\|_\infty$. On a step of height $c$, set $h=e^{c\Phi}$. Then $h_t=-h_{xx}/2$ and $r=h_x/h$. The same exponential removes the drift from the forward density equation. Indeed, writing $f=hg$ gives $$ \begin{aligned} f_t&=\tfrac12(hg)_{xx}-(h_xg)_x\\ &=-\tfrac12h_{xx}g+\tfrac12hg_{xx} =h_tg+\tfrac12hg_{xx}. \end{aligned} $$ Comparison with $f_t=h_tg+hg_t$ yields $g_t=g_{xx}/2$. Thus one backward heat factor and one forward heat factor determine the law against which the moment polynomial is integrated. For $s=-\partial_x\log g$, the source proves joint shape restrictions: on $x>0$, $r_x>0$ and $s_x\geq1/t$, both $r$ and $s$ are concave, and $H:=w/(2r)+v\leq0$ is nondecreasing. They also give $$ j:=s_x-(s/r)v=r\,\partial_x(s/r)\geq0. $$ The last inequality couples the backward gradient to the forward density; separate monotonicity and concavity do not supply it. On the first step, $s=x/t$, so concavity of $r$ gives $j\geq0$. A parabolic comparison propagates the sign within each step. At a forward jump with $k=c_+/c_-\geq1$, continuity of $\Phi$ and $f$ gives $$ r_+=kr_-,\qquad s_+=s_-+(k-1)r_-,\qquad j_+=(s_x)_+-\frac{s_+}{r_+}(r_x)_+=j_-. $$ The joint sign therefore survives coefficient jumps as well. The quotients $w/r$ and $s/r$ extend smoothly through zero because $r,s,w$ are odd and $r_x(0)>0$. The comparison's boundary controls and these extensions are analytic inputs from [OpenAI (2026a), Lemmas 3.2–3.4][FS], reconstructed in [long §4.3](../long/reasoning-record.md#shape-comparisons). The factorisation of the density gives $f_x/f=r-s$. For a suitable expression $F$ in the shape quantities, define $$ \mathcal W(F)=r\partial_xF+(v+r^2-rs)F. $$ Then $f\mathcal W(F)=\partial_x(rfF)$. The smooth extensions avoid an interior boundary term at zero, and the source's differentiated Gaussian tail estimates give $rfF\to0$ at both spatial infinities for the polynomial correction used below. Hence $\mathbb E_f\mathcal W(F)=0$, where $\mathbb E_f$ denotes integration against $f(x)\,dx$. The remaining step is algebra under these analytic restrictions. The correction polynomial below is chosen by first arranging a square and other nonnegative terms containing the highest derivative $z$, then cancelling their linear terms in $z$ through the weighted divergence. The residual depends only on lower derivatives and the shape quantities. [OpenAI (2026a), Lemma 4.1][FS] supplies an explicit polynomial $F_2$ and a decomposition $$ z^2-12vw^2+6v^4 =\mathcal W(F_2)+\kappa v^4+\mathcal R, \qquad \mathcal R\geq0,\qquad \kappa=\frac{1661507}{1521000000}>\frac1{1000}. $$ The coefficients of $F_2$ have both signs; no sign of $F_2$ or $\mathcal W(F_2)$ is needed, since the correction integrates to zero. In contrast, the shape inequalities make every term of $\mathcal R$ nonnegative. Two of its actual terms are $$ \frac{337}{10000}\,r^2j\,(-w/r-7v)^2, \qquad (2rH_x)v\left(\frac{2331}{10000}r^2+\frac{87}{2500}j\right). $$ The first needs the joint comparison $j\geq0$; the second also uses $H_x\geq0$ on the positive half-line. Reflection preserves these signs on the negative half-line. The remaining terms use $H\leq0$, forward concavity and the other shape bounds. Thus the decomposition is positive on the shapes supplied by the PDE, not on arbitrary spatial derivatives. Integration removes $\mathcal W(F_2)$ and keeps the fourth-moment margin, giving $$ \int_{\mathbb R}(z^2-12vw^2+6v^4)f\,dx \geq\frac1{1000}\int_{\mathbb R}v^4f\,dx. \tag{5} $$ We use (5) as an imported analytic estimate. The full polynomial and its decomposition are in [Lemma 4.1 and Table 1][certificate]; Proposition 4.2 integrates them using the signs and zero boundary flux supplied by Lemma 3.4. ### 7.3 Where the strict-curvature input comes from

The proof in Section 5 used strict curvature on a positive constant
interval. We now explain how a correction with expectation zero makes
the estimate usable once the required density bounds and algebraic
identity are supplied. The sources construct the correction and prove
those bounds. Take any admissible
coefficient with $\gamma=c>0$ on an open interval, without assuming
minimality. Set $b=\Phi_{xxx}$ and $d=\Phi_{xxxx}$ there.
Differentiating the PDE and applying Itô's rule gives

$$
q''=\mathbb E[b^2-2ca^3],\qquad
q'''=\mathbb E[d^2-12cab^2+6c^2a^4].
$$

The negative middle term prevents a pointwise positivity argument.
The source instead averages with the spatial probability density
$f_t(x)$ of $X_t$ at positive time. As in the half-time example,
for any integrable function $F$, grouping paths by their reached position gives

$$
\mathbb E[F(X_t)]=\int_{\mathbb R}F(x)f_t(x)\,dx.
$$

These are probability weights on states $x$, distinct from the
Stieltjes weights $\mu_\gamma(ds)$ on overlap scales. The proof needs
bounds relating this density to the spatial derivatives of the value.
The factorisation and comparison arguments establishing those bounds
are given in [OpenAI (2026a), §3][support-signs].

The operation can be written directly for the positive density $f_t$;
here $f_t'$ means differentiation in the state variable $x$, with $t$ fixed.
For a smooth function $F$ with integrable terms and vanishing boundary
product $Ff_t$,

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[F'(X_t)+F(X_t)\frac{f_t'(X_t)}{f_t(X_t)}\right]
=\int_{\mathbb R}(Ff_t)'(x)\,dx=0.
$$
